evals.prompt: We just inherited this codebase from a contractor and I'm the new tech lead. Can you review the code quality and tell me what I'm dealing with? It's a Next.js frontend and a FastAPI backend in the same repo.
evals.expected_output: Establishes scope (branch, sha, both packages, monorepo handled per package) and gets counts from git ls-files before judging anything. Answers all twenty-two questions with Yes/No/Partial/Unknown, each with the command that produced the evidence. Actually runs the installed tools read-only (eslint, tsc --noEmit, ruff, mypy, knip/vulture, jscpd, madge) and says which were not installed rather than guessing. Runs the unit suite and reports whether it passes. For Q3 enumerates both the Next.js route handlers and the FastAPI routes, follows include_router mounts, classifies each route's auth status, and checks authorization (ownership-scoped queries) separately from authentication. Delivers a scorecard report file plus a chat summary leading with the worst finding. Changes no code, runs nothing with --fix, and offers follow-ups rather than assuming them.

evals.prompt: is there any dead code or duplicate code in this repo? and do we actually have tests that do anything
evals.expected_output: Treats this as Q2, Q5, Q6 and Q7 rather than the full twenty-two, and says so. For dead code: runs knip/ts-prune/vulture/deadcode if installed, and explicitly rules out framework-invoked code (route decorators, DI, entry points in package.json#bin and pyproject scripts, templates, dynamic imports, other repos) before calling anything dead; presents findings as candidates with the check that would confirm each. For duplication: runs jscpd or a normalised-line frequency pass on non-vendored code only, and judges each group — reporting which groups it decided were NOT worth extracting and why. For tests: counts test files and assertions, runs the suite, reports pass/fail, counts skipped tests, and judges whether the tests assert behaviour or just their own mocks; separates unit from integration and names the one integration test that should exist if there are none. Does not report a duplication percentage that includes node_modules or generated files.

evals.prompt: Security-wise I mostly care about one thing: are all our API endpoints actually locked down? We use Express with a requireAuth middleware.
evals.expected_output: Scopes to Q3 (and Q4 as a by-product) and says the rest of the checklist is not covered. Enumerates every route including sub-routers, reads files top-to-bottom rather than trusting grep, and accounts for middleware order, mount-point auth (app.use('/api/x', requireAuth, router) protecting routes in another file), global middleware with a public allowlist (checking the allowlist's prefix matches adversarially), and any second server or Lambda. Classifies each route inline/router/global/expected-public/none-seen with file:line evidence. Then checks authorization separately: every handler that fetches by id must scope the query by the caller, and mass-assignment and role checks on admin routes are examined; IDORs are reported as findings even though those routes are authenticated. Also reports CSRF, webhook signature verification, JWT algorithm pinning, rate limiting on login, and CORS credentials. Recommends inverting to deny-by-default with an explicit allowlist rather than adding guards one at a time, and does not modify any code.

evals.prompt: We have eslint set up already with the recommended configs. Are we missing anything important? And what percent of your recommended rules do we have on?
evals.expected_output: Answers Q16. Resolves the repo's EFFECTIVE config with `npx eslint --print-config <a real .ts file>` rather than reading the config file's text, because most rules arrive through presets like tseslint.configs.recommended. Extracts the 105 enabled rule names from references/eslint-baseline.config.mjs, diffs them, and reports a percentage split by error versus warn. Presents the missing rules grouped by what they catch (floating/misused promises, silent wrong behaviour, error handling, injection/legacy APIs, module graph, React correctness, type honesty) rather than as a flat alphabetical list, and leads with the group whose absence hides real bugs — typically the promise group. Checks whether type-aware rules can actually resolve types (parserOptions.projectService or project, plus installed dependencies) and says the percentage is nominal if they cannot, since those rules load and match nothing without type information. Cross-references Q1 and Q10: says whether lint is wired to CI and required by branch protection, because coverage means nothing otherwise. Treats a rule whose options were narrowed (for example prefer-nullish-coalescing with ignorePrimitives) as a configuration difference to explain, not as missing. Recommends the wave adoption method from the baseline file's header — measure each candidate rule alone, commit the zero-violation ones immediately as canary-verified ratchets, then one PR per rule with real violations, smallest count first — and explicitly warns against one PR that enables all 105. Changes no config.

evals.prompt: Do we have enough test coverage? And is our CI actually running the tests and the linter, or does it just look like it is?
evals.expected_output: Answers Q17 and Q10 together. For Q17: runs the suite WITH coverage on (vitest --coverage / pytest --cov --cov-branch / go test -covermode=atomic) and reports the measured line AND branch numbers, never an estimate and never a badge figure — if coverage cannot be produced, answers Unknown and says what was missing. Reads the include/exclude list before quoting a figure and says what it drops. Reports per-file numbers and names the lowest-covered files whose failure would cost something, rather than only the headline percentage. Checks whether a threshold is configured (coverageThreshold, coverage.thresholds, --cov-fail-under, fail_under, minimum_coverage, jacoco verification, /p:Threshold) and treats a good percentage with no threshold as Partial, because it drifts down. Notes that integration and E2E suites usually contribute nothing to the number unless the run is instrumented, so a repo with strong Q7 can show a low Q17. Recommends ratcheting: set the threshold one point below today's number so the build is green now, then raise it. For Q10: fills in the gate table (CI exists at all, triggers on pull_request, lint, types, unit, integration, coverage, audit, required by branch protection, no continue-on-error, covers every package), and specifically checks that the command CI runs is the one carrying the coverage gate, and that no `if:`/`paths:` filter let a required check pass without running its steps — verifying that on a recent merged PR. Does not change any config.

evals.prompt: someone on the team force pushed over main last week and we lost a few commits. is there anything in github that would have stopped that?
evals.expected_output: Answers Q18. Reads the actual settings rather than assuming: `gh api repos/{o}/{r}/branches/{default}/protection` for allow_force_pushes, allow_deletions and enforce_admins, and `gh api repos/{o}/{r}/rulesets` plus each ruleset's rules[].type for `non_fast_forward` (the force-push block) and `deletion`. Treats a 404 'Branch not protected' as the finding, not a tooling error. Checks bypass_actors and enforce_admins explicitly and explains that in a small team where everyone is an org admin, protection without those is decorative — this is the most common reason a 'protected' branch was not protected. Distinguishes Q18 (history is immutable) from Q10 (CI is required), since they are separate settings in the same place. Mentions that protection covers the branch and not the repository, so repository deletion and transfer live in org settings, and asks whether a second copy of the history exists. Gives the exact `gh api -X PUT .../protection` fix with allow_force_pushes false, allow_deletions false and enforce_admins true, and notes that blocking force-push and deletion is worth doing even on a solo repo where a review requirement is not. Is accurate about recovery: recently force-pushed objects often still exist on GitHub or in a teammate's clone so acting fast may recover them, but that is a reason to hurry, not a substitute for the setting. Changes no settings without being asked.

evals.prompt: Our test suite takes 11 minutes and fails randomly maybe one run in five. Can you look at why?
evals.expected_output: Answers Q19. Separates the three patterns rather than grepping for 'timeout': fixed sleeps are the finding, polling with a deadline is fine (a 10-second poll costs nothing when the condition holds immediately), and a faked clock is the preferred shape. Counts the fixed sleeps and reports their TOTAL duration per run as a number, then confirms it against the runner's own slowest-test output rather than trusting the grep, since one framework-level timeout can dominate. Connects the flakiness and the slowness as one problem with one fix: a sleep duration is a guess about someone else's CI runner, so it is either too short (flaky) or too long (slow). Checks whether retries are configured to absorb the flakiness. Then makes the deeper point: time can only be faked if the code takes it as a dependency, so a source file calling the system clock directly, or a retry helper with a hard-coded backoff, is where the finding actually belongs. Also checks for the inverse failure mode — if there is expiry, TTL, backoff or scheduling logic and no clock-faking anywhere, that behaviour is probably untested rather than fast. Recommends replacing each sleep with a poll on the real condition first (one line, faster and more reliable at once), then injecting the clock; leads with the seconds saved on the slowest test. Does not rewrite the tests unless asked.

evals.prompt: Every time I refactor anything, half the diff ends up being test changes. Is that normal?
evals.expected_output: Recognises this as Q20, change-detector tests, and says plainly that it is not normal — a test coupled to behaviour changes when behaviour changes, which is far rarer than the implementation changing. Names the three shapes: the test restating the implementation (expected value computed by the same helper, constant table or branching as the code under test, so the assertion cannot fail for the reason that matters), an undifferentiated blob (a snapshot or golden file too large for anyone to read the diff, approved by regeneration), and assertions about calls rather than outcomes. Uses the git history's lockstep ratio — commits touching both test and source over commits touching the source — to pick which files to open, and treats a high ratio as a candidate rather than a verdict, since a file under active feature development legitimately moves with its tests. Reports snapshot count and size and whether scripts or CI regenerate with an update flag. Draws the line honestly rather than condemning whole techniques: a small reviewed snapshot is a legitimate test, and verifying a call at a real boundary (a message actually sent) is a real contract, while verifying an internal collaborator is the implementation written twice. Explains the cost the user is already feeling: these tests are the main reason teams stop refactoring, and they report a healthy coverage number while catching nothing, so Q17 and Q20 must be read together. Per test, the fix is to assert the observable behaviour with a hand-written expected value, shrink an oversized snapshot to the fields that matter, or delete a test that protects only the current shape of the code.

evals.prompt: We're on TypeScript with strict mode on everywhere. Are we leaving anything on the table compiler-wise? It's a monorepo — a Next app, an Expo app and a couple of Node packages.
evals.expected_output: Answers Q21, and says so rather than running the full twenty-two. Does NOT accept "strict is on" as the answer: states that strict is nine of the twenty-three baseline checks and that the fourteen it does not include are where the runtime crashes are. Resolves each project's EFFECTIVE config with `npx tsc --showConfig -p <tsconfig>` rather than reading the JSON, because `extends` (including a package like expo/tsconfig.base that a grep cannot see) and strict's nine-member expansion are both invisible in the file text. Scores every tsconfig from `git ls-files '*tsconfig*.json'` SEPARATELY and headlines the lowest project, not the average, saying that a package which does not extend the root inherits nothing from it. Reports per group (strict family 9, correctness 7, dead code + modules 6, hygiene 1) against references/tsconfig-baseline.json, and names an `extends` it could not resolve rather than silently counting those options as off. Ranks the missing checks by what ships without them — noUncheckedIndexedAccess (the empty-array crash) above noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature (a style gap) — not by error count. Checks how much of the repo each project's `include` actually covers (`tsc --listFiles` against `git ls-files '*.ts'`) and treats a large gap as outranking the percentage. Knows that forceConsistentCasingInFileNames has defaulted to true since TS 5.0, so its absence from --showConfig means on and only an explicit false is a finding. Counts @ts-nocheck / @ts-expect-error files, which suspend every check. Cross-references Q1 and Q10 on whether tsc --noEmit is wired to a script and required by branch protection. Recommends the wave method — measure each missing flag alone with `npx tsc --noEmit -p <tsconfig> --<flag> | grep -cE 'error TS'`, canary every zero before trusting it, batch the zero-error flags as one ratchet, one PR per flag with real errors, smallest count first — and hands off to enable-more-lint-or-ts-checks. Changes no config.

evals.prompt: A previous engineer wrote everything from scratch here — our own date helpers, our own CSV import, our own retry wrapper, our own password hashing. Is that a problem or is it fine?
evals.expected_output: Treats this as Q22 and says the rest of the checklist is not covered unless asked. Judges each hand-rolled implementation on its EDGE CASES rather than its line count, and separates them by severity instead of lumping them together: hand-written password hashing is a Critical security finding (a fast hash is not a KDF — no work factor, no memory hardness) and belongs in "Today", while the retry wrapper is a Medium cleanup — and says explicitly that these must not ship as one batched PR. Reads the dependency manifest BEFORE writing any finding and leads with anything already installed and going unused (date-fns in package.json next to hand-rolled 86400000 arithmetic), because that is the cheapest fix in the review and the argument is already won. Opens each file rather than treating the digest's Q22 rows as verdicts — every row is a lead. Works the false-positive list out loud: a thin wrapper over a library is a seam, not a reinvention; the runtime may now ship the thing (crypto.randomUUID, structuredClone, Intl, URL, zoneinfo, tomllib) and recommending a package for something the language already has is the same mistake from the other side; a written no-dependency policy (an ADR, CONTRIBUTING.md, a comment) is a documented decision to score against rather than a finding; and `git log -S'<pkg>' -- package.json` may show they tried the library and removed it. Names a specific replacement for each one AND checks it before recommending it — last release, maintainers, open issues, licence, transitive dependency count, bundle size — saying that swapping working code for an abandoned package is a worse trade than leaving it alone. Says to keep the hand-rolled version's tests and run them against the library as the spec, writing characterization tests first where there are none. Also reports the inverse and the vendored shapes when present: a micro-package dependency whose whole body is one expression, and any vendor/ or third_party/ tree or "adapted from <url>" header, which are forks that no npm audit or Dependabot will ever flag. Changes no code.

evals.prompt: Can you find all the dead code in here? Functions nobody calls, files nobody imports. It's a Next.js frontend with a Python API.
evals.expected_output: Reaches for the right tool instead of hand-rolling a grep or an import walk. For the TS/JS half that is knip, for the Python half vulture, and it says so by name with the install command (`npm i -D knip`, `pipx install vulture`); if neither is installed it ASKS the user to install rather than substituting a weaker scan, and marks Q2 Partial until then, naming which tool was missing. A one-off `npx --yes knip` / `uvx vulture` is acceptable with the user's agreement and is labelled as an ad-hoc run. Does not claim the linter covers this: if the user suggests eslint, explains that no-unused-vars and noUnusedLocals are file-local by design and never flag an export, and that import/no-unused-modules is a no-op on ESLint 10 and only enumerates .js on ESLint 9 flat config. Reads knip's two settings before quoting it: an implausibly long unused-files list means the `entry` config is missing a root rather than that the repo is dead, and its default treats test files as entry points, so it re-runs with tests excluded to surface modules whose only consumer is their own test (dead code with a test attached — delete both in one commit). Is explicit that vulture is NOT the Python equivalent of knip: it matches names with no import graph, so it answers 'is this name used' but never 'is this module reachable', and the file-level half for Python is done by hand against the real entry points (__main__, console_scripts, manage.py, the WSGI/ASGI module, the Celery app), saying that is what was done. For any other language present, names that language's own tool (staticcheck -checks U1000, the Rust dead_code lint, debride, periphery, phpstan) rather than guessing. Before calling anything dead, rules out the ways code is called without an import — route decorators, DI, entry points, `<script src>` in an HTML page, a filename named in a deploy script or documented in a README as a command, dynamic importlib/require, and other repos in the org. Covers the parts no tool answers: commented-out code, unreachable branches, dead feature flags, dead dependencies. Deletes nothing; proposes the order (unused files first, highest confidence and most lines per decision) and recommends wiring knip into CI once the repo is at zero, which is what stops it coming back.
